intro: In the middle movement of La Mer, woodwind phrases flicker above plucked strings and quick harp figures. The biggest waves break apart; the ending belongs to a solo flute and a few high string harmonics.

sections.label: A · Soft winds and plucked strings
sections.mNote: Short wind phrases hover above scattered harp and string notes

sections.label: B · Longer phrases, quick replies
sections.mNote: The phrases expand, then break into smaller exchanges

sections.label: C · Winds and strings gather again
sections.mNote: Quick figures pass through winds and strings towards the crescendo

sections.label: Coda · Harps, then a solo flute
sections.mNote: Harp figures and wind fragments fade into high string harmonics

cues.title: A few bright drops
cues.text: Soft chords in cor anglais, clarinets and bassoons hover above plucked cellos and basses. Harp figures and little bell-like notes punctuate the gaps. The violins answer in short chords, divided into several parts.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, movement II, printed p. 174. The bell part is marked glockenspiel, with celesta permitted as an alternative. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/b/b6/IMSLP15420-Debussy_-_La_Mer_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A supple rhythm
cues.text: Debussy puts a qualification beside Allegro: dans un rythme très souple, in a very supple rhythm. Short accents and triplets keep tilting the phrases across the beat. The little figures are quick; the pulse has room to bend.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, movement II heading, printed p. 174. Cross-rhythms are discussed by Susan Key, https://www.laphil.com/works/la-mer.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Proofs at Eastbourne
cues.text: In July 1905 Debussy takes the proofs of La Mer to the Grand Hotel in Eastbourne. Writing to his publisher Jacques Durand, he finds that “the sea unfurls itself with an utterly British correctness”.
cues.evidence: Debussy to Jacques Durand, Eastbourne, summer 1905; the letter and his arrival on 23 July are cited in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_mer_(Debussy), Background and composition.

cues.title: Paris, October 1905
cues.text: Camille Chevillard conducts the Lamoureux Orchestra in the première of La Mer on 15 October 1905. The Paris audience receives it coolly. Three years later, Debussy conducts the work himself and wins an enthusiastic reception.
cues.evidence: Jacob Greenberg’s Boston Symphony programme note gives the 1905 première and Debussy’s Paris performances in January 1908: https://www.bso.org/works/la-mer

cues.title: A tune changes hands
cues.text: A short phrase can move from strings to woodwinds before it has settled into a tune. Debussy keeps altering its rhythm as it passes. The harps and percussion add small, bright replies between the orchestral phrases.
cues.evidence: Jacob Greenberg describes the movement’s short melodic cells, rhythmic transformations and exchanges between orchestral sections: https://www.bso.org/works/la-mer. This note concerns the movement’s recurring manner of writing.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Harps after the swell
cues.text: The strings soften and the wind phrases grow shorter. Harp glissandos rise and fall around a quiet clarinet solo, marked très doux — very gentle. The closing pages keep shedding instruments.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, printed pp. 218–222, beginning at rehearsal 39: paired harp glissandos, clarinet solo, horns and reduced strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Flute and harmonics
cues.text: On the last page, a solo flute leaves a small curling phrase above the held strings. Six first violins play harmonics, barely touched; a harp and a few bell notes glint around them. The bass stays quiet to the end.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, printed p. 222: flute solo, six first violins in harmonics, harp, glockenspiel and sustained lower strings, mostly ppp.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The harps emerge
transitions.from: C · Winds and strings gather again
transitions.to: Coda · Harps, then a solo flute
transitions.how: The late crescendo recedes under En retenant, holding back. The double basses sustain while the upper strings fall silent. At rehearsal 39, the harps sweep in opposite directions, horns hold quiet notes, and a solo clarinet begins a gentle phrase. The bass continues underneath this much smaller ensemble.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, printed pp. 216–218, leading into rehearsal 39. The established coda boundary places the closing retreat.

source.title: Debussy, La Mer · Durand full score, plates D. & F. 6532 / 6838
source.locator: Movement II, printed pp. 174–222: divided and plucked strings at the opening, clarinet and harp glissandos at rehearsal 39, flute and violin harmonics on the last page. The score offers celesta as an alternative to glockenspiel.

timeline.note: Cor anglais, clarinets and bassoons hold soft chords above plucked lower strings; harps and glockenspiel add single notes.
Cor anglais and flute pass short phrases between them while the strings move in quick fragments.
Winds and strings gather into longer phrases, with harps and percussion ringing through the orchestra.
Harp glissandos surround a quiet clarinet phrase, with held horns and low strings beneath it.
A solo flute curls above harps, glockenspiel and the harmonics of six first violins.

composer.epithet: He trusted his ear over the rules — “pleasure is the law” — and made the piano, the flute and the orchestra sound new.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and went to prison for it, and there he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

His teachers could not make him out. Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, found “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament” in January 1874; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Years later, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud around 1890, he put his position plainly: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
